newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northeast spot power steady amid cool weather.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northeast spot power steady amid cool weather.

text.p: Physical electricity prices in the northeastern U.S. ended Friday steady against Thursday's level amid forecasts of very cool weather in the northern part of the region, market sources said.

Thursday's brief outage of New York Power Authority's 965 megawatt (MW) Indian Point 3 nuclear power plant in Buchanan, N.Y., continued to support daily prices because it disrupted delivery to certain bulk power customers, market sources said.
"The outage was unexpected. It interrupted scheduling into New England on Friday," one East Coast trader said.
Indian Point 3 was expected to resume full output Friday.

In the New York Power Pool (NYPP), peak, non-firm prices of electricity in the western portion of the grid was quoted near $17.75 a megawatt hour (MWh) for the weekend and $18.75 for Monday, compared with Thursday's quote of $18.25-$18.75.
Non-firm electricity for peak demand periods in eastern NYPP was assessed near $20.00 for the weekend and $21.00 for Monday, compared with Thursday's range of $21.00-$22.00.

In the New England Power Pool (NEPOOL), non-firm power during heavy load hours at Northeast Utilities' territory border was quoted near $25.50 a MWh for the weekend and $28.50 for Monday, compared with a quote of $28.50 and $29.00 on Thursday for Friday delivery.
Non-firm, off-peak NEPOOL electricity at NU's border for the weekend was assessed at $17.50 for the weekend and $19.50 for Monday, compared with $18.00-$20.00 on Thursday.
There were market discussions that a baseload NEPOOL coal unit was shut today, forcing the operator to fire up a natural gas fired unit to compensate for the loss of the coal unit.

Although 20 to 30 Fahrenheit degree weather in the northern part of NYPP and NEPOOL was expected to trigger some heating demand over the weekend, many participants downplayed its significance in the long run.
"We'll see more seasonal weather before we hit winter. We're still in a shoulder month," said one NYPP trader.
